A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolution of ribosome biogenesis has involved multiple ancient gene duplications and domain shufflings that have led to the emergence of a number of new enzymatic activities.

the two domains TSR3 and TSR5 (DUF1963) are unified into a novel superdomain, with TSR3 being a novel superfamily, and TSR5 a novel domain superfamily, both having a conserved role, but with different functions in rRNA maturation.
we have identified and characterized the two domains with novel rRNA-processing activities and established their roles in the complex evolution of the ribosome biogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complex evolution of rRNA biogenesis in eukaryotic cells was enabled by the incorporation of bacterial proteins with novel RNA-processing functions, in addition to those of archaeal origin.

the evolution of ribosome biogenesis is a complex process involving a large number of proteins, many of which are still uncharacterized, and that the emergence of the eukaryote-specific rRNA maturation pathway involved the acquisition of novel proteins from the bacterial world, as well as the cooption of existing proteins for novel functions.

the complex evolution of rRNA biogenesis is reflected by a large set of novel, biochemically unexplored proteins with diverse roles in rRNA processing, and that computational methods provide a useful framework for identifying and analyzing them.
